content:
Good UI/UX design is less about how a screen looks and more about whether a person can finish what they came to do without thinking about it. A buyer comparing apartments on Golf Course Extension Road should find the floor plan and price-on-request button in seconds. A clinic patient should book a slot without calling anyone. A finance manager in a GCC office should read a dashboard without a training session. At TopWebExpert, UI/UX design is a stage of its own, done before development, and it is where we catch most of the problems that would be expensive to fix in code.

What You Receive at the End

Clients often ask what they are actually paying for, so we start with the deliverables. A full UI/UX engagement typically produces:

  • Research summary: findings from user interviews, analytics review and a look at how competitors handle the same tasks.
  • User flows: diagrams of each key journey, such as signing up, searching, booking or paying.
  • Wireframes: low-detail layouts of every screen, agreed before visual design starts.
  • High-fidelity designs in Figma: final screens for mobile and desktop, including empty, loading and error states.
  • Clickable prototype: a link you can open on your phone and share with your team or investors.
  • Design system: colours, type, spacing, buttons, form fields and components, documented so developers build consistently.
  • Developer handover: annotated specs, exported assets and a walkthrough call with whoever will build it.

For smaller projects, such as redesigning a single checkout or onboarding flow, we scope down to the pieces that matter.

How We Research Your Users

We talk to real users, not just stakeholders. For a B2B SaaS product that might mean five or six interviews with customers over video. For a consumer app it can mean sitting with users at your store or clinic and watching them try the current flow. We pay attention to local habits that change design decisions:

  • Many users switch between Hindi and English, so labels need to be short and clear in both.
  • A large share of traffic comes from budget Android phones with smaller screens, so tap targets and text size matter.
  • People expect to pay through UPI and to get updates on WhatsApp, and flows should match that.
  • OTP login is familiar; long passwords and email verification loops cause drop-offs.

The Design Process and Timeline

  1. Week 1: Kickoff and audit. A workshop at our Sohna Road office in Sector 49 or at your premises, review of analytics and the existing product, and agreement on the key user tasks.
  2. Weeks 2–3: Research and flows. Interviews, competitor review and user flow diagrams.
  3. Weeks 3–5: Wireframes and testing. Low-fidelity screens, tested with a handful of users to find confusion early.
  4. Weeks 5–8: Visual design. High-fidelity screens and the clickable prototype, with two structured review rounds.
  5. Weeks 8–9: Design system and handover. Component library, specs and a handover session with the development team.

A focused redesign of one flow can take three to four weeks. A new product with many user roles may take longer than nine.

Accessibility Is Part of the Brief

We design to WCAG 2.1 AA as a baseline: sufficient colour contrast, readable font sizes, visible focus states, labelled form fields and layouts that work when users enlarge text. This helps older users and people with low vision, and it also makes screens easier to use in bright sunlight on a phone, which matters for field staff and delivery users.

How We Check the Design Before It Is Built

Every design goes through usability testing with real users, even if only five people, because that is usually enough to show the biggest problems. We also run a heuristic review against established usability principles, check every screen for missing states, and confirm with your developers that each component is practical to build in your chosen framework. It is far cheaper to move a button in Figma than in production code.

Ownership of the Design Files

You own the final designs, the Figma files and the design system after payment. We transfer the files to your Figma workspace, so your team or any future agency can keep working from them. Fonts and stock images are licensed in your name where needed.

Common UX Mistakes

  • Designing for the founder's taste rather than the user's task.
  • Starting visual design before the flows are agreed, which leads to repeated rework.
  • Forgetting error, empty and offline states, so developers invent them on the fly.
  • Asking for too much information at sign-up.
  • Handing developers static images with no specs or component library.

When This Service Is Not the Right Fit

If you only need a few banners or a quick visual refresh of an existing website, a full UX process is more than you need; a graphic design task will do. It is also not a fit if the product decisions are already locked and there is no room to change flows based on what users tell us, or if there is no time for your team to review designs.

FAQs About UI/UX Design

What is the difference between UI and UX?

UX is how the product works: the steps, the order of information and how easy it is to finish a task. UI is how it looks: layout, colour, type and components. We do both, and UX comes first.

How is the cost worked out?

It depends on the number of screens and user roles, how much research is needed, and whether you need a full design system. After a free consultation we send a fixed quote based on an agreed scope.

Can you redesign our existing app without rebuilding it?

Often, yes. We can work within your current framework and design system, and prioritise changes that improve the most-used flows first.

Can our in-house developers build from your designs?

Yes. Our handover includes specs, assets and a walkthrough, and we stay available for questions during development.

Do you only work with companies in Gurugram?

No, but being local helps with in-person research. Clients from Cyber City, Sector 29 or anywhere in Gurgaon can join workshops at our office easily.
